extracted.intended_audience: general readers, law students, and legal practitioners interested in administrative law and rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and limits governing agency rulemaking procedure and judicial review under the Administrative Procedure Act, as articulated by the Supreme Court in Vermont Yankee v. NRDC. Useful for evaluating what procedures agencies must follow and what procedures courts may (or may not) require.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA and statutory mandate set maximum procedural requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal Administrative Procedure Act of 1946 and an agency's statutory mandate from Congress establish the maximum requirements for an agency's rulemaking (and adjudicative) process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies are bound by the procedures required by the APA and by any additional procedures mandated by their enabling statutes; courts should not read into the APA procedural obligations beyond what the statute provides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency discretion to grant additional procedural rights
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency may grant additional procedural rights in the regulatory process (within constitutional and statutory limits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies voluntarily may provide more procedure (e.g., extended comment periods, additional hearings), but such choices must still comply with constitutional constraints and their statutory authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts generally may not impose additional procedures on agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: While federal agencies are free to grant additional procedural rights in the exercise of their discretion, reviewing courts are generally not free to impose them if the agencies have not chosen to grant them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A court should not require procedures that the agency did not provide or that are not required by statute/APA; doing so risks exceeding the limits of judicial review of agency action. The Vermont Yankee holding was directed at restraining courts (not agencies) from adding procedural requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on courts imposing their own notion of 'best' procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: A reviewing court cannot 'impose upon the agency its own notion of which procedures are 'best' or most likely to further some vague, undefined public good'; to do so would exceed the limits of judicial review of agency action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicit judicial-limit principle—courts must avoid substituting their policy or procedural preferences for those chosen by agencies or set by statute. The decision criticized the D.C. Circuit for overstepping by advancing judges' policy preferences through procedural requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core APA notice-and-comment obligations (notice and statement of basis and purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA's requirements that agencies issue a notice of proposed rulemaking and a statement of basis and purpose represent the baseline procedural obligations for informal rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vermont Yankee suggested courts should adhere to the original understanding of these APA requirements, though subsequent cases and circuits have not always applied Vermont Yankee as limitingly. Practitioners should ensure agencies issue adequate notice and an adequate statement of basis and purpose when conducting notice-and-comment rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy of the administrative record to support a rule
rubrics_metrics.description: A rule must be adequately supported by the administrative record; Vermont Yankee was remanded for the circuit court to determine whether the Table S-3 rule was adequately supported by the administrative record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reviewing a rule substantively, courts examine whether the administrative record provides adequate support for the agency's conclusions; lack of adequate support can lead to remand. The NRC later revised the rule and the revised regulation was subject to further judicial review (e.g., Baltimore Gas & Elec. Co. v. NRDC).

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence of hybrid rulemaking despite Vermont Yankee
rubrics_metrics.description: While Vermont Yankee limited courts' ability to impose additional procedures, courts have continued to embrace hybrid rulemaking to some degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vermont Yankee 'tipped the scales back to formalism,' but it did not eliminate all instances where courts require quasi-adjudicative procedures or other hybrid processes; agencies and practitioners should be aware that hybrid procedures remain a live (and fact-specific) possibility in some circuits.
